facts.statehood_note: One of the original 13; Rhode Island ratified the U.S. Constitution on May 29, 1790, the 13th and last of the former colonies to do so. It was also the first colony to renounce allegiance to the British Crown, on May 4, 1776. In 2020 voters dropped "and Providence Plantations" from the state's official name. It is the smallest state by area.
facts.nickname: The Ocean State (also called Little Rhody)
borders: Atlantic Ocean (Rhode Island Sound and Block Island Sound)
facts.name_origin: The name comes from Aquidneck Island: in 1524 the explorer Giovanni da Verrazzano compared an island here to the Greek island of Rhodes, and the name was officially used from 1644. The exact origin is not certain.

government.legislature: Rhode Island General Assembly, which meets in the Rhode Island State House in Providence (people sometimes call the legislature "Smith Hill" after the neighborhood)
government.chambers: Rhode Island Senate (38 senators, 2-year terms) and Rhode Island House of Representatives (75 members, 2-year terms), sizes set in the constitution since 2003
government.executive: Governor (4-year term, elected every four years since 1994; no one may serve more than two full terms in a row). The governor and lieutenant governor are elected separately, not on one ticket.
government.courts: Rhode Island Supreme Court (5 justices: a Chief Justice and four Associate Justices), the state's court of last resort.
government.local: Rhode Island has 5 counties but no county governments; local government is run by 39 municipalities (8 cities and 31 towns).
government.constitution: Rhode Island was governed by its 1663 Royal Charter until 1843. After the Dorr Rebellion, voters approved a new constitution in November 1842 (in effect May 1843) that gave the vote back to Black men, outlawed slavery, and kept the Narragansett from voting. The current constitution was ratified by voters in November 1986.
government.kid_line: "All free governments are instituted for the protection, safety, and happiness of the people." (Rhode Island Constitution, Article I, Section 2)

long_ago.about: The Narragansett controlled the land west of Narragansett Bay and parts of today's Connecticut and Massachusetts, and spoke an Algonquian language. Their sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi gave Roger Williams the land for Providence in 1636.

The Pokanoket Wampanoag lived at Sowams, near today's Warren, and on the Bristol peninsula, with their center at Mount Hope. Wampanoag women farmed the Three Sisters (corn, beans, and squash) and gathered wild foods and shellfish, producing up to 75 percent of the food, and families traced their belonging through mothers.
The Niantic are named among the Native peoples of the Rhode Island area along with the Narragansett, Wampanoag, Pequot, and Nipmuc.
Nipmuc and Pequot peoples also lived in and around what became Rhode Island; Roger Williams urged Massachusetts not to enslave Pequot women and children for life after the Pequot War.

today.about: Rhode Island's one federally recognized tribe, recognized in 1983, with an 1,800-acre reservation in Charlestown, where its August powwow, called the oldest recorded powwow in North America, is held.

first_peoples.today_note: The Narragansett Indian Tribe is the only federally recognized tribe in Rhode Island. From 1880 to 1884 the state tried to end the tribe's status and sold its lands; the tribe won back about 1,800 acres in 1978 and federal recognition in 1983. The two federally recognized Wampanoag tribes today are in Massachusetts.
sites: Narragansett Indian Reservation (Charlestown), home of the annual August powwow
Mount Hope (Bristol), center of the Pokanoket Wampanoag and the place Metacom was killed in 1676
Great Swamp Fight site, where colonial militia destroyed a Narragansett fort in 1675

history.event: The Narragansett live west of Narragansett Bay, and the Pokanoket Wampanoag live around Mount Hope Bay.
Italian explorer Giovanni da Verrazzano sails by and compares an island here to the Greek island of Rhodes.
Roger Williams, banished from Massachusetts for his religious ideas, founds Providence on land he gets from Narragansett sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi.
Anne Hutchinson and others found Portsmouth (1638), and Newport follows in 1639. In 1643 Williams publishes A Key into the Language of America, a study of the Narragansett language.
The colony passes the first anti-slavery law in America, but there is no evidence it was ever enforced.
King Charles II grants a Royal Charter that sets up the colony's government and guarantees religious liberty.

King Philip's War: on December 19, 1675, colonial militia destroy a Narragansett fort in the Great Swamp Fight, killing hundreds of non-fighters. Metacom (King Philip), the Wampanoag sachem, is killed at Mount Hope on August 12, 1676, and many surviving Native people are sold into slavery.
The General Assembly makes slavery legal, and the slave trade, tied to making rum, makes Newport and Providence rich; by 1755 enslaved people are 8% of Providence's population.
On June 10, 1772, Providence residents burn the British customs ship Gaspee. On May 4, 1776, Rhode Island becomes the first colony to renounce allegiance to the British Crown.

The First Rhode Island Regiment, the first African American military unit to fight for the United States, fights in the Battle of Rhode Island on August 29, 1778. In 1780 free Black Newporters found the Free African Union Society.

The Gradual Emancipation Act (March 1) says children born to enslaved mothers after that date cannot be held in bondage, though enslavers kept them until age 21 (boys) or 18 (girls). People already enslaved stay enslaved.
On May 29, Rhode Island becomes the 13th state to ratify the U.S. Constitution.
Samuel Slater sets up Slater Mill in Pawtucket, powered by the Blackstone River, an early step in America's Industrial Revolution.
Black men lose the right to vote in 1822, and race riots strike Providence's Hard Scrabble (1824) and Snow Town (1831) neighborhoods.

In the Dorr Rebellion, people demand the vote for all men. Voters approve a new constitution in November 1842 that gives the vote back to Black men and outlaws slavery, but keeps the Narragansett from voting.
Rhode Island is the first Union state to send troops when Abraham Lincoln asks; it sends 23,700 soldiers, and 1,685 die.

trailblazers.name: Canonicus and Miantonomi
trailblazers.text: These Narragansett leaders gave Roger Williams the land for Providence in 1636 and Canonicus signed a peace treaty with the colonists. Miantonomi was later captured during a conflict and killed in 1643 by Uncas's brother.

trailblazers.name: Roger Williams
trailblazers.text: Williams founded Providence as a safe place for people of any faith and argued that government should not control religion. He learned the Narragansett language and questioned colonists taking land without buying it, but during King Philip's War he also led a committee that sold Native captives.

trailblazers.name: Anne Hutchinson
trailblazers.text: In Boston, Hutchinson led religious meetings for women and men and challenged local ministers, so Massachusetts banished her in 1637. In 1638 she helped found Portsmouth, Rhode Island, and she is remembered as a figure in religious freedom and women's history.

trailblazers.name: Metacom (King Philip)
trailblazers.text: Metacom became sachem in 1662 and built alliances to stop colonists from taking more Wampanoag land. He led King Philip's War and was killed at Mount Hope on August 12, 1676.

trailblazers.name: The First Rhode Island Regiment
trailblazers.text: The First Rhode Island Regiment was the first African American military unit to fight for the United States. Its soldiers fought in the Battle of Rhode Island on August 29, 1778.

trailblazers.name: Newport Gardner
trailblazers.text: Newport Gardner helped found the Free African Union Society in Newport in 1780, the first African mutual aid society in America, where free Black residents supported one another.

trailblazers.name: Christiana Carteaux Bannister
trailblazers.group: African American and Narragansett woman, businesswoman and abolitionist
trailblazers.text: Born in North Kingstown to a mixed African American and Narragansett family, she became a successful hairdresser with her own salons in Boston and later Providence. A strong abolitionist, she used her money to support the 54th Massachusetts, a regiment of Black Civil War soldiers, and to help her husband, Edward Bannister, paint full-time. She founded the Home for Aged Colored Women in Providence for elderly Black women shut out of other homes.

landforms: Narragansett Bay and its more than 30 islands (largest: Aquidneck, Conanicut, and Prudence)
Block Island, about 12 miles off the south coast
waters: Atlantic Ocean, Rhode Island Sound, and Block Island Sound
geography.regions: Rhode Island is the smallest state, built around Narragansett Bay and its islands, with mainland towns around the bay and Block Island out in the Atlantic.

ecosystems.name: Narragansett Bay estuary
ecosystems.about: New England's largest estuary covers about 147 square miles; tiny drifting plants called phytoplankton form the base of the food chain, and one survey found 246 kinds of plankton.

ecosystems.name: Shellfish shores
ecosystems.about: Wampanoag women gathered shellfish along with wild plants as part of a seasonal cycle of fishing, planting, harvesting, and hunting.

science.weather: Rhode Island is open to hurricanes; damaging storms include the 1938 New England hurricane, Carol (1954), Donna (1960), and Bob (1991).
science.resources: The Blackstone River powered Slater Mill (1793), and Providence became known for textiles, machine tools, jewelry, and silverware; in colonial times the slave trade and rum making brought wealth. Today health services are the largest industry, followed by tourism and manufacturing.
science.highlight: Narragansett Bay is a ria, a drowned river valley: as sea level rose, the ocean flooded old river valleys, making a bay full of islands. It is New England's largest estuary, where river water mixes with salty ocean water.

g3_ss.title: Rhode Island's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Providence, Newport, and the student's town; learn the General Assembly (Senate 38, House 75), the governor, and why Rhode Island has counties without county governments; discuss the motto "Hope."

g3_ss.title: Rhode Island's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Narragansett and Wampanoag; Three Sisters farming and shellfish gathering; the Narragansett Indian Tribe and its August powwow today.

g3_ss.title: Rhode Island Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Timeline cards for Canonicus and Miantonomi, Roger Williams, Anne Hutchinson, the First Rhode Island Regiment, and Newport Gardner; students write how each stood up for an idea.

g45_ss.title: Rhode Island's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Narragansett and Wampanoag homelands, women's farming and matrilineal families, and Roger Williams's Key into the Language of America as a source to read carefully.

g45_ss.title: A Colony of Conscience and of Slavery
g45_ss.plan: Providence 1636, Hutchinson and Portsmouth, the 1652 anti-slavery law, the 1663 charter, King Philip's War and the Great Swamp Fight, and Newport's slave trade.

g45_ss.title: Rhode Island 1772–1865
g45_ss.plan: The Gaspee, May 4, 1776, the First Rhode Island Regiment, the Free African Union Society, ratification in 1790, Slater Mill, the Dorr Rebellion and 1842 voting rights, and the Civil War.

g3_sci.title: Life in the Bay
g3_sci.plan: What lives in Narragansett Bay, from plankton to fish; build a simple food chain.

g3_sci.title: Hurricane Ready
g3_sci.plan: How hurricanes form, the 1938 hurricane story, and a family storm kit.

g3_sci.title: Islands and Shores
g3_sci.plan: Make maps of Aquidneck, Prudence, and Block Island; compare beaches, marshes, and rocky shores.

g45_sci.title: How a Bay Is Made
g45_sci.plan: Rising seas, drowned river valleys (rias), and salt and fresh water mixing in an estuary; a salinity layering experiment.

g45_sci.title: Water Power and the Mill
g45_sci.plan: How the Blackstone River turned Slater Mill's machines; build a model waterwheel and discuss who worked in mills.

g45_sci.title: Plankton: The Base of the Bay
g45_sci.plan: Use microscopes or images to study plankton, and learn why scientists count the 246 kinds found in the bay.
